alt: Answers need two parts: what the source teaches and what difference it makes in society. A table gives a key source and social impact for neighbours, amanat, backbiting, arrogance and jealousy.
caption: “Social impact” questions need the effect on society, not just the teaching.

alt: The prescribed Bukhari Hadith links faith to the neighbour’s safety. Five rights follow: safety from harm, kindness and gifts, help in need, respect for privacy and patience. A note cites Qur’an 4:36 and the Hadith about Jibril (AS) advising on neighbours.
caption: Safety is the minimum right: faith is linked to how a neighbour is treated.

alt: Forms of amanah around a centre: goods left for safekeeping, as Ali (RA) returned on the night of the Hijrah, secrets, one’s job, public office and money, one’s body and abilities, and the neighbour’s safety, privacy and reputation. A note gives Qur’an 4:58 and the signs of a hypocrite.
caption: Amanah includes secrets, jobs, promises and responsibilities, not only money.

alt: Saying about someone what they would dislike is backbiting if it is true and slander if it is not. Qur’an 49:12 compares backbiting to eating a dead brother’s flesh. Muslims should defend the absent person; scholars allow limited exceptions such as reporting wrongdoing or giving an honest warning when asked.
caption: Backbiting is wrong even when it is true.

alt: Arrogance began with Iblis refusing to prostrate to Adam (AS). Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people (Sahih Muslim; Qur’an 31:18); liking good clothes is not arrogance, because Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Arrogance divides people; humility supports equality.
caption: Arrogance means rejecting truth and looking down on people, not liking good things.

alt: When seeing another’s blessing, hasad wants them to lose it, resents Allah’s decree and leads to hatred; it is forbidden. Ghibtah wishes for the same good without wanting them to lose it, as in the Hadith of the two cases of wealth spent rightly and wisdom; it is allowed. The cure is contentment, gratitude and du’a.
caption: Wishing for the same blessing is allowed; wishing someone to lose it is not.
